11778.title: Game Environment versus Level Design
11778.heading: Game Environment versus Level Design
11778.content:
Game-environment design establishes the world's visual character through architecture, objects, lighting, color, and mood. It makes the setting readable and emotionally coherent rather than merely filling empty space with decoration.

Level design emphasizes the challenges, routes, rules, and pacing the player encounters in that setting. The disciplines overlap because spatial appearance can guide action, but an attractive environment does not automatically create a playable level.

11781.title: Game Environment Artist Scope
11781.heading: Game Environment Artist Scope
11781.content:
A game environment artist constructs the visible world and its atmosphere. The work can include terrain, architecture, set dressing, surface appearance, lighting, and the arrangement that communicates the game's setting to the player.

The exact scope depends on studio size. A large team may divide concept art, props, modeling, texturing, and lighting among specialists, while an independent team may ask one artist to move across most of the asset pipeline.

11784.title: Game Entity
11784.heading: Game Entity
11784.content:
A game entity is a datum or collection of data representing an object, character, quantity, or state of affairs in the game world. A building, character, score, pile of gold, or traffic-light state can all be entities.

Entities make the world computable. Their values and attributes supply the state on which events, processes, and conditions operate.

11787.title: Game Economy
11787.heading: Game Economy
11787.content:
A game economy is a system dominated by reinforcing loops in which resources, time, or power are exchanged or converted for a perceived gain in value. Its activity comes from players choosing among immediate use, trade, production, and investment.

Sources, stocks, converters, currencies, and sinks form its flows. The system must remain dynamic while resisting [[Economic Inflation]], [[Economic Stagnation]], and uncontrolled [[Arbitrage]].

11790.title: Game Ecology
11790.heading: Game Ecology
11790.content:
A game ecology is a system dominated by balancing loops in which parts exchange resources while constraining one another. The parts may each contain reinforcing loops, yet their aggregate interaction tends toward metastable dynamic balance.

Ecologies need not simulate biology: combat, inventory, factions, and social competition can share this structure. A healthy ecology is neither frozen nor runaway; it remains resilient and perturbable by [[Meaningful Decision|meaningful player decisions]].

11793.title: Game Difficulty
11793.heading: Game Difficulty
11793.content:
Game difficulty is the demand a game places on a player's current skill and understanding. It can arise from timing, prediction, coordination, strategy, endurance, or the need to learn relationships within the system.

Increasing difficulty is one possible shape for a game, not a universal measure of quality. A challenging experience can build confidence through mastery, while other games use [[Game Resistance|resistance]] to support reflection, exploration, or listening rather than conquest.

11796.title: Game Development Team
11796.heading: Game Development Team
11796.content:
A game development team is a coordinated system of people whose design, programming, art, sound, writing, production, testing, and other skills produce a game. Its effectiveness depends more on shared vision and interaction than on merely assembling expert parts.

Successful teams maintain mutual respect, clear roles, open communication, accountability, local authority, and room to learn from mistakes. They address risks and destructive behavior while avoiding extended crunch and unnecessary design thrashing.

11799.sourceSearchName: game development phases game development phases
11799.title: Game Development Phases
11799.heading: Game Development Phases
11799.content:
Game development commonly moves through concept, preproduction, production, alpha, beta, and release. These phases mark changing emphasis and evidence rather than a waterfall sequence, because design, building, and testing continue to loop throughout.

Concept validates the vision and core loops; preproduction clarifies features, assets, cost, and schedule; production builds the game; alpha establishes broad playability; beta emphasizes stability and release concerns; release begins learning from the full player population.

An agile phase boundary is evidence-based: preproduction explores fun, tools, budgets, and uncertainty, while production begins when mechanics and pipelines are stable enough for predictable content flow. Short iterations continue inside both phases even though their dominant risks differ.

11802.sourceSearchName: game developer playtest game developer playtest
11802.title: Game Developer Playtest
11802.heading: Game Developer Playtest
11802.content:
A game developer playtest uses peers who understand how games are designed and built. These testers can identify systemic patterns, production risks, and familiar design problems earlier than a general audience might articulate them.

Their expertise can also distort the evidence because developers tolerate roughness and infer missing conventions. Their observations should answer an early design question rather than substitute for tests with the intended players.

11805.sourceSearchName: game detailed design document game detailed design document
11805.title: Game Detailed Design Document
11805.heading: Game Detailed Design Document
11805.content:
A game detailed design document specifies parts, attributes, values, and behaviors precisely enough to implement. It records both the rationale for each part and an operational description that can become code or analog rules.

Quantities should use defined numbers, ranges, equations, or explicit unresolved issues rather than vague adjectives. Linked diagrams, mockups, prototypes, and spreadsheets keep the detail connected to the higher-level [[Game System Design Document|system]] and [[Game Concept Document|concept]] documents.

Detailed documentation is most reliable when it records knowledge demonstrated in the working game and names important unknowns. Writing speculative precision far ahead of implementation hides assumptions and makes the document expensive to maintain as the design emerges.

11808.sourceSearchName: game design synthesis game design synthesis
11808.title: Game Design Synthesis
11808.heading: Game Design Synthesis
11808.content:
Game design synthesis combines ideas and constraints from several disciplines into a consistent playable vision. Programming, art, audio, writing, production, publishing, budget, hardware, and schedule can pull a design in different directions.

Synthesis is not simple compromise. The designer identifies relationships among concerns and finds a solution that still serves the intended player while giving collaborators meaningful ownership of the result.

11811.title: Game Designer
11811.heading: Game Designer
11811.content:
A game designer defines how a game should work and what experience its rules, interface, world, and content should produce. The role includes concept creation, communication, documentation, iteration, and tuning.

Designers work within a team rather than owning every decision. They must understand other disciplines well enough to coordinate constraints and preserve a coherent whole without replacing the specialists who implement art, code, audio, or writing.

11814.heading: Game Design Tracking Spreadsheet
11814.content:
A game design tracking spreadsheet keeps the evolving work visible alongside the design document and schematics. It can separate decisions awaiting discussion, tasks at different horizons, recurring responsibilities, required assets, and completed work.

The structure connects design intent to execution without pretending every future step is known. Updating it after evaluation turns a chosen revision into accountable work for the next prototype.

11817.heading: Game Design Schematic
11817.content:
A game design schematic maps how screens, scenes, states, or moments connect across the player experience. It turns a verbal description into a visible structure that exposes required content, transitions, decisions, and feedback.

The schematic can combine flow diagrams, wireframes, and storyboards according to the current question. Its abstractions should make the next prototype easier to plan rather than imitate finished art.

11820.heading: Game Design Collaboration
11820.content:
Game design collaboration treats the design as knowledge produced with programmers, artists, audio specialists, and testers through a working game. Designers communicate known vision and important unknowns, then participate directly in the team discovering feasible behavior.

Assigning a designer to each core-mechanic team shortens conversations and lets implementation evidence reshape the design. Documents support this collaboration when they record current knowledge rather than speculative detail.

11823.heading: Game Design Brainstorming
11823.content:
Game design brainstorming is a group method for generating many ideas before judging them. Participants emphasize quantity, postpone criticism, welcome unusual proposals, and combine or improve one another's suggestions.

Separating generation from evaluation protects momentum and participation. After the session, the team can compare ideas against player, platform, scope, market, and gameplay requirements.

11826.title: Game Currency
11826.heading: Game Currency
11826.content:
A game currency is a broadly usable resource that mediates exchange without being transformed into the object purchased. Unlike a production input, it can in principle circulate and enable later transactions.

Games often remove spent currency through a [[System Sink]], even when the fiction implies continued circulation. A currency remains useful only while players perceive it as valuable and have meaningful alternatives for spending or saving it.

Currency is a flexible [[Reward]] because its value can be divided and held for later use. The choice to exchange it now or save toward a different opportunity makes the resource a means of enabling future verbs and objects.

11828.title: Game Concept
11828.heading: Document
11828.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Methods]] · [[Game Concept Development]]

11829.title: Game Concept
11829.heading: Game Concept
11829.content:
A game concept is the single driving idea that unifies what players do, how they progress, and what the experience is meant to feel like. It provides a shared reference for selecting systems, content, theme, and style.

A focused concept does not prescribe one player path. It guides [[Second-Order Design]] by defining the intended whole while leaving room for a broad [[Play Space]] and discovery through prototyping.

For commercial discussion, a game concept must be detailed enough to identify the player's role and primary activity, audience, genre, platform, business model, competition modes, progression, world, and broad story direction. It is more developed than a [[Game Idea]] but remains an outline rather than a complete design.

11832.title: Game Crowdfunding
11832.heading: Game Crowdfunding
11832.content:
Game crowdfunding raises development money from many prospective players before the game is finished. Support commonly functions as preordering with rewards rather than as ownership investment.

A successful campaign needs a credible team, persuasive demonstration, clear promises, and continuing communication. It can free a niche project from publisher and retailer pressure while creating direct obligations to funders.

11835.title: Game Context
11835.heading: Game Context
11835.content:
Game context is the collection of images, words, animation, sound, and timing that gives abstract rules a recognizable meaning. Numerical positions and collisions become characters, weapons, dangers, and goals that players can reason about.

Context is not merely decoration around mechanics. It supplies metaphors that help players anticipate how [[Game Part|objects]] behave and why a [[Game Rule]] exists, turning mechanical feedback into an intelligible experience.

11837.title: Game Condition
11837.heading: Document
11837.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Core Mechanics and Internal Economies]]

11838.title: Game Condition
11838.heading: Game Condition
11838.content:
A game condition is a true-or-false test used by mechanics to decide whether an event occurs, a process begins or ends, or a consequence applies. Conditions can inspect entity values, time, location, ownership, or prior events.

Precise conditions prevent ambiguity between design and implementation. Complex behavior is built by combining tests without hiding exceptions that the player cannot learn.

11841.sourceSearchName: game concept document game concept document
11841.title: Game Concept Document
11841.heading: Game Concept Document
11841.content:
A game concept document is a short, high-level, persuasive description of a proposed game. It communicates the concept, player experience, product position, and first outline of the design without becoming a detailed design bible.

It is a living and preferably visual nexus for later documentation. Typical elements include a [[Concept Statement]], target audience, unique selling points, player fantasy, core loops, world, style, scope, and production considerations.

The source's high concept document also identifies the player's role, primary gameplay mode, genre, target machine, revenue approach, licensed material, competition modes, progression, story direction, and game world. These choices make the proposal concrete enough for discussion while postponing detailed mechanics until elaboration.

11842.sourceSearchName: game concept document game concept document

11844.title: Game Component
11844.heading: Game Component
11844.content:
A game component is a reusable behavior object owned by a [[Game Actor]]. It can update, process input, draw, play audio, or expose collision data while relying on the actor for shared transform and lifetime.

Components reduce duplication across unrelated actor types. They also need an explicit interface and update order so several components can modify or consume actor state predictably during the same frame.

11846.sourceSearchName: game collaboration soft skills game collaboration soft skills
11846.title: Game Collaboration Soft Skills
11846.heading: Document

11847.sourceSearchName: game collaboration soft skills game collaboration soft skills
11847.title: Game Collaboration Soft Skills
11847.heading: Game Collaboration Soft Skills
11847.content:
Game collaboration depends on listening, clear explanation, constructive criticism, empathy, negotiation, reliability, and willingness to revise one's own idea. These skills determine whether specialized knowledge can become a coherent shared design.

They are production capabilities rather than personality extras. A technically strong contribution loses value when teammates cannot question, understand, integrate, or build upon it.

11848.sourceSearchName: game collaboration soft skills game collaboration soft skills
11848.title: Game Collaboration Soft Skills
11848.heading: References

11850.title: Game Camera
11850.heading: Game Camera
11850.content:
A game camera determines what portion of the game world the player can see and from what point of view. It may show the whole world, follow a protagonist, remain fixed, or present the world through a first-person perspective.

Camera design changes the perceived relationship between player, character, and world. An overhead view can frame play as strategy, while a first-person view makes the protagonist the lens through which the world is perceived.

11852.sourceSearchName: game class lifecycle game class lifecycle
11852.title: Game Class Lifecycle
11852.heading: Document

11853.sourceSearchName: game class lifecycle game class lifecycle
11853.title: Game Class Lifecycle
11853.heading: Game Class Lifecycle
11853.content:
A game class lifecycle coordinates initialization, the main [[Game Loop]], and shutdown through one owning object. Initialization creates subsystems and loads data; the loop processes input, updates state, and renders; shutdown releases game data before the libraries it depends on.

Keeping those phases explicit makes partial failure manageable. If initialization stops midway, the game can release only the resources that were successfully created rather than relying on process termination.

11854.title: Game Class Lifecycle

11856.sourceSearchName: game character design game character design
11856.title: Game Character Design
11856.heading: Game Character Design
11856.content:
Game character design uses visible form to distinguish characters and communicate the rules that govern them. Shape, color, equipment, posture, and motion can suggest threat, role, ability, or relationship before the player acts.

In fast play, the player must recognize important differences at a glance. Distinct designs therefore support both narrative characterization and the reliable identification of [[Game Part|game objects]] with different behaviors.

Character design also coordinates the intended [[Player-Avatar Relationship]] with model sheets, movesets, back story, behavior, and voice. A compelling character belongs in the game world, supports the required actions, remains memorable, and avoids relying on a stereotype in place of depth.

11857.title: Game Character Design

11858.title: Game Behavior State Machine

11859.sourceSearchName: game behavior state machine game behavior state machine
11859.title: Game Behavior State Machine
11859.heading: Game Behavior State Machine
11859.content:
A game behavior state machine places an agent in one behavior state at a time and defines events or conditions that trigger transitions. States such as patrol, chase, attack, and flee isolate behavior appropriate to different situations.

The model is easy to reason about when transitions remain explicit. Large machines can become tangled, which motivates encapsulating behavior and transitions with the [[State Design Pattern]].

Tags: [[Game Balance and Progression]] · [[Game Balance and Difficulty]]

11862.title: Game Balance
11862.heading: Game Balance
11862.content:
Game balance is a dynamically stable relationship among parts, systems, progression, and players. A balanced game avoids an inherent or insurmountable advantage, preserves several viable strategies, and lets players recover from reasonable risks.

Balance is a property of the whole [[Game-Player System]], not only of numeric equality between parts. It combines designer judgment, [[Playtesting]], player analytics, and mathematical models while keeping the [[Play Space]] perturbable and meaningful.

The source distinguishes competitive balance from player-versus-environment difficulty management. A balanced competitive game avoids dominant strategies and preserves the relevance of skill despite chance; a balanced environmental game keeps perceived difficulty within a credible range as challenge, player power, and experience change.

11864.sourceSearchName: game audio event game audio event
11864.title: Game Audio Event
11864.heading: Document

11865.sourceSearchName: game audio event game audio event
11865.title: Game Audio Event
11865.heading: Game Audio Event
11865.content:
A game audio event is an authored playback definition referenced by a stable name. It can select sounds and control looping, variation, parameters, routing, and effects beyond a single raw file.

Playing the event creates an instance represented by a [[Sound Event Handle]]. The distinction lets many simultaneous instances share one event definition while keeping their position, parameters, playback state, and lifetime independent.

11868.title: Game AI Strategy and Planning
11868.heading: Game AI Strategy and Planning
11868.content:
Game AI strategy and planning selects actions over a longer horizon than immediate movement or local behavior. It may allocate resources, choose objectives, coordinate units, or evaluate candidate plans against changing world state.

The system does not need exhaustive optimality to appear intelligent. Real-time strategy opponents often combine authored priorities, evaluation functions, and limited search so decisions arrive within the game's computational budget.

11871.title: Game Attribute
11871.heading: Game Attribute
11871.content:
A game attribute is a named value that contributes to a part's current state. First-order attributes hold amounts, second-order attributes describe rates of change, and higher-order attributes can describe changes in those rates.

Attribute ranges should be understandable, broad enough to distinguish meaningful states, and reusable across related parts. Every added attribute increases implementation and balance complexity, so it should enable useful behavior or a [[Meaningful Decision]].

11873.sourceSearchName: game asset list game asset list
11873.title: Game Asset List
11873.heading: Document

11874.sourceSearchName: game asset list game asset list
11874.title: Game Asset List
11874.heading: Game Asset List
11874.content:
A game asset list inventories the visual, audio, textual, and other produced materials required by the current design. Each item can record its purpose, owner, status, dependencies, and the prototype or final experience in which it must appear.

Deriving the list from design schematics ties production work to player-facing needs. It also reveals when a proposed interaction depends on more content than the project's time and resources can support.

11875.title: Game Asset List

11876.sourceSearchName: game as conversation game as conversation
11876.title: Game as Conversation
11876.heading: Document

11877.sourceSearchName: game as conversation game as conversation
11877.title: Game as Conversation
11877.heading: Game as Conversation
11877.content:
Game as conversation is a model in which the creator structures a system and the player responds through action. The game presents rules, resistance, and opportunities; the player uses [[Game Verb|verbs]], makes choices, and receives [[Feedback]].

The creator may not be present when play occurs, but design still shapes what can be said and heard. Different games can invite open response, focused interpretation, competition, or a quieter form of listening.

11878.sourceSearchName: game as conversation game as conversation
11878.title: Game as Conversation
11878.heading: References

11880.title: Game Actor
11880.heading: Game Actor
11880.content:
A game actor is a runtime object with identity, state, transform, and an ordered collection of components. It receives input and update opportunities, then delegates specialized work to its attached [[Game Component|components]].

The actor supplies the shared position, scale, and rotation that rendering, movement, collision, and audio components interpret. Its lifecycle also determines when the world registers or removes the object.

11883.title: Galois Group
11883.heading: Galois Group
11883.content:
The Galois group of a root field E over K consists of automorphisms of E that fix K. Its elements permute the roots of the defining polynomial while preserving every field relation.

For the finite root fields in the book, the group order equals the extension degree.

11886.title: Galois Correspondence
11886.heading: Galois Correspondence
11886.content:
The Galois correspondence relates intermediate fields of a root-field extension to subgroups of its Galois group. Larger subgroups fix smaller fields, and normal subgroups correspond to intermediate root fields.

It translates questions about field towers into questions about finite groups.

11888.sourceSearchName: gain share pricing gain share pricing
11888.title: Gain-Share Pricing
11888.heading: Document

11889.sourceSearchName: gain share pricing gain share pricing
11889.title: Gain-Share Pricing
11889.heading: Gain-Share Pricing
11889.content:
Gain-share pricing gives a provider an agreed portion of improvement beyond a baseline. The consumer compares actual performance with historical or standard performance and shares some of the resulting gain through a predetermined formula.

The model rewards the provider for exceeding expected service levels and can be combined with penalties for underperformance. A credible baseline and a clear method for calculating the gain are essential.

11892.sourceSearchName: galileo navigation system galileo navigation system
11892.title: Galileo Navigation System
11892.heading: Galileo Navigation System
11892.content: Galileo is the European Union's satellite-navigation system, created to provide an independently governed civil capability despite free access to GPS. Its medium-Earth-orbit architecture, onboard atomic clocks, and coded signals broadly resemble GPS, while its governance, service definitions, hydrogen-maser standards, and safety-of-life features reflect European priorities. Galileo demonstrates that constellation ownership is also a question of industrial capacity and political autonomy.

11895.title: Fuzzy Weighted Squared Error
11895.heading: Fuzzy Weighted Squared Error
11895.content:
Fuzzy weighted squared error sums the squared distances from observations to cluster centers after weighting each contribution by its membership. It evaluates how well a fuzzy partition fits its prototypes.

The measure can compare a current set of clusters with a proposed merge or drive the iterative updates in fuzzy C-means. Its meaning still depends on the scale and distance used.

11898.title: Gabor Filter
11898.heading: Gabor Filter
11898.content:
A Gabor filter responds to image structure at a particular spatial scale and orientation. A bank of filters produces local energy measurements that capture oriented texture and edge patterns.

Multiple scales and directions make the representation expressive, but also enlarge the feature vector. Pooling or selecting filter responses can retain the most useful texture information while limiting dimensionality.

11901.title: G-Buffer
11901.heading: G-Buffer
11901.content:
A G-buffer is the collection of screen-sized render targets produced by the geometry pass of [[Deferred Shading]]. Its attachments store data such as diffuse color, surface normal, world position, and depth for the nearest visible surface.

The lighting pass reconstructs its calculation from these per-pixel properties without drawing the original meshes again. Attachment formats must balance precision and bandwidth because every visible pixel writes and later reads several values.

11904.content:
Fuzzy subspace clustering stores a matrix of dimension weights in addition to memberships and centers. Each cluster can emphasize attributes on which its members are compact and reduce the influence of irrelevant dimensions.

Weight normalization and a fuzziness-like exponent prevent arbitrary scaling and control concentration. The resulting SubspaceCluster objects publish both representative centers and per-cluster relevance profiles.

11907.heading: Fuzzy State Machine
11907.content:
A fuzzy state machine assigns degrees of membership to multiple behavior states rather than requiring exactly one state to be active. Contributions from states can be blended according to their weights.

The approach supports gradual changes such as becoming increasingly afraid as health falls. It can avoid abrupt thresholds, though blended behaviors need rules that prevent incompatible actions from producing incoherent results.

11910.title: Fuzzy Set
11910.heading: Fuzzy Set
11910.content:
A fuzzy set assigns every element in a universe a membership value between zero and one. Values near one indicate strong membership, values near zero weak membership, and intermediate values express partial belonging.

Unlike a crisp set, membership need not switch at one hard threshold. Several fuzzy sets can describe one attribute through linguistic terms such as low, medium, and high.

11913.title: Fuzzy Partition
11913.heading: Fuzzy Partition
11913.content:
A fuzzy partition covers a data set with clusters whose membership values may lie anywhere between zero and one. Under a probabilistic constraint, the memberships of each observation across all clusters sum to one.

A [[Crisp Partition]] is the special case in which every membership is exactly zero or one. Fuzzy partitions make boundary cases visible instead of hiding them behind one hard label.

The method retains density-based handling of irregular shapes and noise while exposing borderline uncertainty. Its output depends on how uncertain distributions are converted into neighborhood evidence and how fuzzy reachability is aggregated.

11934.heading: Fuzzy C-Means Prototype Update
11934.content:
Fuzzy C-means updates each prototype as a membership-powered weighted average of all records, then recalculates memberships from distances to the updated prototypes. The fuzziness parameter controls how strongly large memberships dominate the center.

Iteration stops when the membership change falls below a threshold or an iteration limit is reached. Coincident points and zero distances need special handling to avoid division by zero in the membership formula.

11937.content:
Fuzzy clustering allows an observation to belong to several clusters with different degrees of membership. It is designed for ambiguous boundaries where a forced one-group assignment would conceal meaningful overlap.

A membership matrix and an objective function connect those degrees to cluster representatives. The added flexibility requires careful choices about how membership is defined and interpreted.

The Cmean implementation stores a fuzzy membership matrix whose entry gives the degree to which one record belongs to one cluster. Initialization allocates the matrix and derives starting memberships from randomly selected centers.

Fuzzy C-means begins with a membership matrix, computes membership-weighted cluster centers, updates memberships from distances to those centers, and repeats until the matrix changes by less than a tolerance.

Every observation can belong partly to several clusters. The method extends K-means but remains sensitive to initialization, the selected number of clusters, the distance measure, and outliers.

11946.title: Fuzzing
11946.heading: Fuzzing
11946.content:
Fuzzing is a testing technique that supplies an application with inputs outside its expected specification to expose crashes, unsafe behavior, or security vulnerabilities. It explores cases that ordinary examples or valid-input tests may never exercise.

The technique is most useful when failures are recorded reproducibly and converted into regression tests after repair. In a cloud service, the test environment should be isolated so malformed traffic does not disrupt production consumers.

Higher temperature helps overcome the [[Fusion Coulomb Barrier]], but a plasma too sparse or too briefly confined still produces inadequate reaction output. Overcoming the barrier is necessary but not sufficient: the fuel also must be confined long enough and at enough density to release useful net energy.

11967.content:

A project can satisfy its written requirements and still disappoint users when unstated context is missing. Continuous contact, prototypes, and observation help reveal those assumptions before they become expensive design failures.

11970.title: Functional Programming
11970.heading: Functional Programming
11970.content: Functional programming organizes computation around functions that transform values, emphasizing explicit inputs and results over hidden mutation. C# supports this style without requiring an entirely functional application: delegates and lambdas represent behavior, LINQ composes transformations, and pure calculations can be separated from database and user-interface effects. The benefit is that central business rules become easier to reason about and test when their dependencies are visible.

11973.title: Functional Morality
11973.heading: Functional Morality
11973.content:
Functional morality is morally acceptable machine behavior achieved without claiming that the machine is a complete moral person. A system can be designed to respect constraints, avoid foreseeable harm, remain within the law, or choose among limited actions using encoded priorities.

This is a practical target for an [[Artificial Moral Agent]] because safety does not require proving consciousness, emotion, or free will. Its limits matter: a functional system may fail outside the situations anticipated by its designers, and its rule-following does not make it responsible for the values chosen. Human oversight and [[Algorithmic Accountability]] remain necessary.

11976.title: Function
11976.heading: Function
11976.content:
A function assigns each element of a domain exactly one element of a codomain. The image is the set of outputs actually attained, which may be smaller than the codomain.

Homomorphisms are functions with the additional requirement that algebraic operations are preserved.

A total function assigns an output to every domain element, whereas a partial function may be undefined for some inputs. A function can also be viewed as a relation in which each input appears with exactly one output.

11979.title: Functional Honesty
11979.heading: Functional Honesty
11979.content: Functional honesty means a function's contract reveals the conditions under which it can produce a valid result. The book revises a discount calculation to accept a `ValidDiscount` value rather than an arbitrary decimal, moving a business constraint into the input contract. This is distinct from purity: a function can deterministically compute a result from an invalid percentage while still being a poor representation of the domain rule.

It can be applied top-down from desired function to structure or bottom-up as Structure-Behavior-Function. In [[Systemic Game Design]], it connects the intended player experience to [[Game System|systems]] and the [[Game Part|parts]] that implement them.

11985.title: Function Transformation
11985.heading: Function Transformation
11985.content: Function transformations derive new graphs from a known graph. Adding a constant outside the function shifts vertically, replacing $x$ by $x-h$ shifts horizontally, multiplying the output scales vertically, and replacing $x$ by a multiple scales horizontally. Negative factors create reflections across an axis. Their order matters when several transformations are combined.

12000.title: Function Composition
12000.heading: Function Composition
12000.content:
Function composition applies one function and then another, with (g ◦ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Composition is associative when the domains and codomains match.

Automorphisms form groups under composition because identities and inverse functions preserve the structure.

Composition is defined when the outputs of the first function lie in the domain of the second. Its associativity allows a chain of transformations to be grouped without changing the resulting mapping.

12003.title: Function Component
12003.heading: Function Component
12003.content:
A function component is a JavaScript or TypeScript function that accepts props and returns React elements. It provides a reusable piece of interface without requiring a component class.

Hooks such as [[React useState Hook|useState]] and [[React useEffect Hook|useEffect]] give function components local state and lifecycle-related effects. A TypeScript function-component type can associate a defined props interface with the function.

12006.title: Function Argument
12006.heading: Function Argument
12006.content:
A function argument is the value supplied to a parameter when an R function is called. Arguments may be positional or named, and names improve clarity when a call has several options.

Validation near the function boundary can produce useful errors before invalid arguments contaminate later calculations.

12009.title: Function Approximation
12009.heading: Function Approximation
12009.content:
Function approximation replaces a complicated or unavailable analytic function with a simpler function that is easier to evaluate, differentiate, or integrate.

The source data may be tabulated measurements or costly calculations. [[Interpolation]] requires the approximation to match known values, while [[Least Squares Approximation]] allows discrepancies so noisy data can be modeled without passing through every point.

12012.title: Fun
12012.heading: Fun
12012.content:
Fun is a voluntary, generally nonconsequential, positively valenced form of sustained engagement. It may arise through sensory, cognitive, social, emotional, or cultural interaction as long as the demands fit the individual's current [[Interactivity Budget]].

Not every engaging game experience is fun in a simple pleasurable sense, but fun experiences are engaging. A design can aim for tension, sadness, or reflection while still supporting meaningful action and continued attention.

A filtering helper can receive `Func<decimal, bool>` as a criterion, then apply it to each discount value without knowing how the criterion was written. Passing such values makes behavior configurable at a call site and supports higher-order functions.

If there are $n$ locations and $m$ times, its data table has $n m$ rows even when some values are missing. The `spacetime` package represents this layout with STF or [[STFDF Object|STFDF]], enabling systematic spatial slices, temporal series, and space-time plots.

12021.title: Full Backup
12021.heading: Full Backup
12021.content:
A full backup copies the entire selected fileset each time the backup job runs. Every resulting backup set contains both unchanged and changed items from that scope.

Restoration is straightforward because one set contains the complete snapshot, but repeatedly copying everything consumes more time and storage than change-based schemes. The simplicity can be valuable when fast, dependable recovery matters more than backup efficiency.

12027.title: Fuel Use Across Climb and Cruise
12027.heading: Fuel Use Across Climb and Cruise
12027.content: Total airborne fuel use combines the fuel consumed while climbing with the flow accumulated during cruise. Pressure altitude, outside temperature, engine speed, and flight duration all influence the result, and ground-operation fuel must be added separately. Segmenting the calculation makes deviations easier to monitor through [[In-Flight Fuel Monitoring]].

12030.title: Fuel Efficiency Unit Conversion
12030.heading: Fuel Efficiency Unit Conversion
12030.content: The book's fuel-efficiency quantities are distance per fuel volume: mi/gal and km/L. Converting mi/gal to km/L multiplies by kilometers per mile and by gallons per liter, the latter being the reciprocal orientation of a liters-per-gallon factor. Miles and gallons cancel separately. This is a compound ratio conversion, not merely a conversion of miles; both parts of the measure must preserve their positions. See [[Reciprocal Conversion Factors]] and [[Compound Rate Unit Conversion]].
